stem:
A 40-year-old male presents with severe pain, photophobia, and blurred vision following an inadvertent
injury with a palm leaf. Slit-lamp exam shows a central corneal ulcer with feathery, finger-like extensions and
satellite lesions. What is the most appropriate initial topical antimicrobial treatment?
rationale:
Fungal keratitis following vegetative/agricultural trauma (e.g., palm leaf) classically presents with feathery margins and
satellite lesions. Topical Natamycin 5% suspension is the first-line drug of choice.

stem:
A 28-year-old contact lens wearer presents with excruciating right eye pain out of proportion to clinical
findings, photophobia, and a ring-shaped corneal stromal infiltrate. Microscopic examination of corneal
scrapings shows double-walled cysts. What is the pathognomonic clinical feature of this condition?
rationale:
Acanthamoeba keratitis in contact lens wearers presents with severe pain disproportionate to signs and pathognomonic
radial keratoneuritis (radial perineural infiltrates along corneal nerves).

stem:
A 22-year-old student presents with recurrent episodes of red eye, photophobia, and foreign body sensation.
Slit-lamp examination reveals a branching epithelial defect with terminal bulbs that stains brightly with
fluorescein. Corneal esthesiometry shows reduced corneal sensation. Which medication must NEVER be
prescribed?
rationale:
Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated in active HSV dendritic epithelial keratitis as they suppress local immunity,
causing the ulcer to transform into a destructive geographic/amoeboid ulcer.

stem:
A 19-year-old male complains of progressive distortion of vision and frequent changes in astigmatic
cylindrical glass prescription. On examination, looking downward causes a V-shaped notch on the lower
eyelid. What is the name of this characteristic eyelid sign?
rationale:
Munson's sign is the V-shaped indentation/notching of the lower eyelid caused by the ectatic conical cornea when the
patient looks downward in Keratoconus.

stem:
Which layer of the human cornea contains an active Na+/K+-ATPase metabolic pump responsible for
maintaining corneal deturgescence (relative dehydration) and clarity, but possesses NO regenerative
capability?
rationale:
The corneal endothelium is a single hexagonal cell layer with an active Na+/K+-ATPase pump that maintains corneal
dehydration. Endothelial cells cannot divide or regenerate after birth.

stem:
A 55-year-old patient with long-standing Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy develops painful bullae on the corneal
surface due to severe corneal decompensation. Which surgical procedure replaces ONLY the diseased
posterior corneal layers (endothelium and Descemet's membrane)?
rationale:
DSAEK/DMEK replaces only the diseased endothelial layer and Descemet's membrane, leaving the patient's healthy
anterior stroma intact, unlike full-thickness Penetrating Keratoplasty.

stem:
A patient presents with a semi-dense corneal opacity involving the anterior half of the corneal stroma,
through which the pupil and iris details are partially visible. How is this corneal scar classified?
rationale:
A Macula is a semi-dense corneal opacity involving the anterior stromal layers through which underlying iris features can
still be partially discerned (Nebula is faint, Leucoma is dense white).

stem:
Which corneal dystrophy is inherited in an Autosomal Recessive pattern and is characterized by
mucopolysaccharide deposits in the stroma that extend all the way to the limbus?
rationale:
Macular corneal dystrophy is the only major autosomal recessive stromal dystrophy (Granular and Lattice are autosomal
dominant) and features diffuse stromal clouding extending to the limbus.

stem:
A 30-year-old welder works without protective goggles and wakes up at midnight with severe bilateral ocular
pain, blepharospasm, and lacrimation. Fluorescein staining reveals diffuse punctate epithelial erosions (SPK).
What is the primary cause?
rationale:
Photokeratitis (Welder's flash / Snow blindness) is caused by absorption of UV-B radiation by the corneal epithelium,
causing shed epithelial cells and diffuse painful punctate erosions.

stem:
Which organism is clinically notorious for its ability to breach and invade a completely intact, uninjured
corneal epithelium?
rationale:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae (along with Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Listeria) can penetrate intact corneal epithelium
without prior epithelial trauma.

stem:
During a slit-lamp exam of a 16-year-old keratoconus patient, vertical fine stress lines are noted in the deep
stroma and Descemet's membrane that disappear upon applying gentle pressure to the globe. What are these
lines called?
rationale:
Vogt's striae are vertical stromal stress lines in keratoconus that transiently disappear when external digital pressure is
applied to the eye.

stem:
A golden-brown or greenish iron ring deposited in Bowman's layer surrounding the base of the cone in
keratoconus is known as:
rationale:
Fleischer's ring is an epithelial iron deposit at the base of the cone in keratoconus (distinguish from Kayser-Fleischer ring
in Wilson's disease, which is copper in Descemet's membrane).

stem: What is the total average refractive power of the human cornea?
rationale:
The cornea contributes approximately +43 D (about 70%) to the eye's total fixed refractive power of +60 D (the crystalline
lens contributes ~+15 to +20 D).

stem:
A patient with neurotrophic keratitis secondary to trigeminal nerve (CN V1) palsy develops a non-healing
corneal epithelial defect. What is the primary underlying pathophysiology?

options.C: Loss of sensory innervation and trophic factors

rationale:
Trigeminal nerve injury causes loss of corneal sensation and essential neurotrophic factors, leading to epithelial
breakdown, impaired healing, and painless neurotrophic ulcers.

stem:
A 60-year-old female presents with severe dry eyes, rheumatoid arthritis, and a melt of the peripheral
corneal stroma. What is this condition called?
rationale:
Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) is an autoimmune crescentic stromal melting process at the limbus strongly
associated with systemic collagen vascular diseases like Rheumatoid Arthritis.

stem:
A 68-year-old diabetic patient presents with gradual, painless decrease in vision. Slit-lamp exam shows
opacification located directly at the posterior pole of the crystalline lens along the visual axis. The patient
reports severe glare when driving towards sunlight. What type of cataract is this?
rationale:
Posterior Subcapsular Cataract (PSC) lies directly in the visual axis at the posterior nodal point, causing prominent glare
and disproportionate vision loss in bright light (when pupil constricts).

stem:
A 6-week-old infant is brought with bilateral white pupillary reflexes (leukocoria). Systemic workup reveals
galactokinase deficiency. What is the classic morphological pattern of cataract associated with galactosemia?
rationale:
Galactosemia (due to galactokinase or GALT deficiency) causes accumulation of dulcitol in the lens, producing a
pathognomonic central 'oil-droplet' cataract.

stem:
A 35-year-old patient with Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) undergoes ocular evaluation.
Copper deposition in the anterior lens capsule produces which characteristic named cataract?
rationale:
Wilson's disease causes copper deposition beneath the anterior lens capsule, producing a stellate brown-green
'sunflower' cataract (as well as KF rings in Descemet's membrane).

stem:
A 25-year-old man presents with difficulty relaxing his hand grip after a handshake, frontal balding, and
bilateral cataracts consisting of highly reflective polychromatic crystals. What is the underlying systemic
condition?
rationale:
Myotonic dystrophy is characterized by myotonia, muscle wasting, frontal balding, and pathognomonic 'Christmas-tree'
polychromatic crystalline lens opacities.

stem:
A 70-year-old patient undergoes uncomplicated phacoemulsification with posterior chamber intraocular
lens (PCIOL) placement. One year later, vision gradually blurs. Examination shows proliferation of residual lens
epithelial cells forming 'Elschnig's pearls' across the posterior capsule. What is the treatment of choice?
rationale:
Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO / Elschnig's pearls) is the most common late post-op complication of cataract
surgery, treated non-invasively with Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy.

stem:
During phacoemulsification, the posterior lens capsule ruptures and a large nuclear fragment falls deep
into the vitreous cavity. What is the immediate, correct surgical step?

options.A: Attempt to retrieve the nucleus with phaco probe in the vitreous
options.B: Instill topical pilocarpine to constrict pupil
options.C: Perform anterior vitrectomy to clear the wound, insert IOL if support allows, and refer for Pars Plana Vitrectomy
options.D: Abort surgery and close skin without removing vitreous
options.E: Inject high-density viscoelastic and perform scleral expression immediately

rationale:
If nuclear fragments drop into the vitreous, never chase them with the phaco handpiece in the vitreous cavity. Perform
anterior vitrectomy to clear vitreous from the anterior segment/wound, place IOL if sulcus support exists, and refer to a vitreoretinal
surgeon for Pars Plana Vitrectomy.

stem:
A 50-year-old male receives a heavy blunt blow to his right eye from a tennis ball. Slit-lamp exam reveals a
rosette-shaped (star-shaped) cortical opacity and a circular ring of iris pigment deposited on the anterior lens
capsule. What is this pigment ring called?
rationale:
Vossius' ring is a ring of iris pigment imprinted onto the anterior lens capsule following blunt ocular trauma due to sudden
compression of the iris against the lens.

stem: In the optical SRK formula for IOL power calculation (P = A - 2.5L - 0.9K), what does 'L' represent?

options.C: Axial length of the eye in millimeters

rationale:
In the SRK formula (P = A - 2.5L - 0.9K), P is IOL power, A is the manufacturer's A-constant, L is axial length in mm, and
K is average corneal curvature in Diopters.

stem:
A hypermature senile cataract in which the entire cortex has liquefied into a milky fluid, allowing the dense
brown nucleus to sink to the bottom of the capsular bag, is termed a:
rationale:
A Morgagnian cataract is a hypermature cataract where cortex liquefaction allows the heavy, hard brownish nucleus to
float freely or sink to the bottom of the capsule.

stem: Which Purkinje-Sansom image is ABSENT in an aphakic eye (an eye lacking a crystalline lens)?
rationale:
Images 1 and 2 are formed by the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces. Images 3 and 4 are formed by the anterior and
posterior lens surfaces, so images 3 and 4 are completely absent in aphakia.

stem:
A 14-year-old boy with high stature, arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, and aortic root dilation presents
with bilateral ectopia lentis (lens subluxation). In which direction is the lens most commonly displaced in
Marfan syndrome?
rationale:
In Marfan syndrome, ectopia lentis is typically bilateral, symmetrical, and displaced upwards and temporally
(superotemporal displacement due to fibrillin-1 defect; contrast Homocystinuria which displaces downwards and nasally).

stem:
On the first post-operative day following cataract surgery, a patient presents with severe limbus-to-limbus
corneal edema, fixed dilated pupil, and sterile anterior chamber exudate without pain. Vitreous is clear. What is
the most likely diagnosis?
rationale:
TASS is a sterile non-infectious inflammatory reaction caused by toxic substances entering the AC during surgery (e.g.,
denatured viscoelastics, detergent residues), presenting within 12-24 hours with severe corneal edema and AC reaction without
vitreous involvement.

stem:
What type of intraocular lens (IOL) fixation is preferred when the capsular bag and posterior capsule are
completely destroyed or absent during trauma?

options.C: Scleral-fixated IOL or Anterior Chamber IOL (ACIOL)

rationale:
When posterior capsular support is absent, an Anterior Chamber IOL (ACIOL) or Scleral-Fixated Posterior Chamber IOL
(SFIOL) is indicated.

stem:
A 62-year-old hypermetropic female presents to the emergency room with sudden, agonizing right eye pain,
severe frontal headache, nausea, and colored halos around lights. Examination reveals a fixed, mid-dilated
vertically oval pupil, corneal edema, and an IOP of 64 mmHg. What is the immediate, mandatory systemic drug
to lower IOP rapidly?
rationale:
IV Mannitol 20% (1.5-2 g/kg) is an hyperosmotic agent administered urgently in acute angle-closure glaucoma to
dehydrate the vitreous body and lower dangerously elevated IOP rapidly.

stem:
What is the definitive, curative surgical/laser procedure of choice for Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma once
the acute attack has been medically controlled?

options.B: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) in both eyes

rationale:
Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) creates a bypass for aqueous from the posterior to anterior chamber, eliminating
pupillary block. Crucially, prophylactic LPI must be performed on BOTH eyes as the anatomical predisposition is bilateral.

stem:
A 3-month-old infant is brought by his parents due to excessive tearing (epiphora), photophobia, and
blepharospasm in both eyes. Examination under anesthesia reveals enlarged corneas (diameter 13.5 mm) with
horizontal curvilinear breaks in Descemet's membrane. What are these breaks called?
rationale:
Haab's striae are horizontal or concentric curvilinear ruptures in Descemet's membrane resulting from corneal stretching
in primary congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos).

stem:
What is the initial surgical procedure of choice for Primary Congenital Glaucoma when the cornea is clear
enough to allow visualization of the anterior chamber angle structures?
rationale:
Goniotomy is the procedure of choice for primary congenital glaucoma if the cornea is clear, incising Barkan's membrane
to open the trabecular meshwork (trabeculotomy is done if cornea is cloudy).

stem:
A 58-year-old open-angle glaucoma patient is started on Latanoprost eye drops. What is the primary
mechanism of action by which prostaglandin analogs reduce intraocular pressure?

options.C: Constriction of ciliary body blood vessels
options.E: Decreasing aqueous humor production at ciliary epithelium

rationale:
Prostaglandin analogs (Latanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost) reduce IOP primarily by remodeling extracellular matrix in
ciliary muscle, thereby enhancing uveoscleral aqueous outflow.

stem:
A patient with Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) exhibits a classic arcuate visual field defect
extending from the blind spot and arching over the fixation point into the nasal field. What is this field defect
called?
rationale:
Bjerrum's scotoma (arcuate scotoma) is a classic glaucomatous field defect caused by damage to arcuate nerve fiber
bundles, extending from the blind spot around fixation into the nasal area.

stem:
Which class of topical anti-glaucoma medication is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in patients with a
history of bronchial asthma, severe COPD, or second/third-degree heart block?
rationale:
Topical non-selective beta-blockers like Timolol undergo systemic absorption via nasolacrimal mucosa, potentially
precipitating fatal bronchospasm in asthmatics/COPD patients and severe bradycardia.

stem:
On gonioscopic examination, a hyperpigmented line is identified running anterior to Schwalbe's line in a
patient with pigment dispersion syndrome. What is this line called?
rationale:
Sampaolesi line is a prominent line of dark pigment deposited on or anterior to Schwalbe's line on gonioscopy, seen in
pigment dispersion syndrome and pseudoexfoliation glaucoma.

stem:
What is the gold standard instrument for precise measurement of Intraocular Pressure (IOP) in adult clinical
practice?
rationale:
Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT) attached to the slit lamp is the universally recognized gold standard for
measuring IOP based on the Imbert-Fick principle.

stem:
A 65-year-old male with open-angle glaucoma presents with a cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) of 0.85, disc
hemorrhages, and neuroretinal rim thinning. Which region of the neuroretinal rim is characteristically lost
FIRST in early glaucomatous optic neuropathy?

options.C: Inferior and Superior poles (ISNT rule compliance loss)

rationale:
Glaucomatous damage preferentially affects the inferior and superior poles of the optic disc (violating the normal ISNT
rule where Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal rim thickness).

stem:
A patient presents with elevated IOP, flaky white fibrillar pseudoexfoliative material deposited on the
anterior lens capsule, pupil margin, and trabecular meshwork. What is the primary diagnosis?
rationale:
Pseudoexfoliation syndrome (PEX) features systemic fibrillar amyloid-like material deposited on the anterior lens capsule
('bulls-eye' pattern), iris, and trabecular meshwork, causing secondary open-angle glaucoma.

stem:
A patient develops high IOP 3 weeks after severe blunt trauma to the eye. Gonioscopy reveals widening of
the ciliary body band due to a tear between longitudinal and circular fibers of the ciliary muscle. What is this
condition?
rationale:
Angle-recession glaucoma occurs post-blunt trauma due to laceration between longitudinal and circular ciliary muscle
fibers, leading to late trabecular meshwork sclerosis and secondary glaucoma.

stem: What is the hallmark clinical finding of Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG)?

options.A: IOP of 10 mmHg with corneal edema
options.B: IOP >30 mmHg with normal visual fields
options.C: IOP consistently <= 21 mmHg with glaucomatous optic disc cupping and field defects
options.D: Intermittent IOP spikes at night with deep AC
options.E: IOP of 50 mmHg without optic nerve damage

rationale:
Normal Tension Glaucoma (NTG) is defined by progressive glaucomatous optic nerve cupping and visual field loss
occurring despite intraocular pressure remaining consistently within normal range (<= 21 mmHg).

stem:
A patient with advanced ischemic CRVO presents 3 months later with severe ocular pain, red eye, elevated
IOP of 50 mmHg, and arborizing neovascular vessels on the anterior surface of the iris (rubeosis iridis). What
type of glaucoma has developed?
rationale:
Neovascular glaucoma ('100-day glaucoma') is triggered by severe retinal ischemia (e.g., ischemic CRVO, proliferative
diabetic retinopathy) causing VEGF release, rubeosis iridis, and fibrovascular closure of the AC angle.

stem:
A 65-year-old hypertensive male experiences sudden, complete, painless loss of vision in his right eye.
Ophthalmoscopy reveals a pale, milky-white ischemic retina with a distinct 'cherry-red spot' at the macula.
What is the primary diagnosis?
rationale:
CRAO presents with sudden, profound, painless monocular vision loss. The retina becomes pale/edematous, while the
fovea transmits underlying choroidal vascularity, creating a pathognomonic 'cherry-red spot'.

stem:
What is the most common anatomical site of origin for an embolus causing Central Retinal Artery
Occlusion (CRAO)?

options.C: Deep veins of the lower extremity

rationale:
Hollenhorst plaques (cholesterol emboli) originating from atherosclerotic disease at the carotid artery bifurcation are the
commonest source of retinal artery emboli.

stem:
A 60-year-old patient presents with sudden 'blood and thunder' fundus appearance featuring widespread
flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, tortuous dilated veins, and cotton wool spots. What is the
diagnosis?
rationale:
CRVO classically produces a 'blood and thunder' fundus with extensive flame hemorrhages in all four quadrants, vein
engorgement, optic disc edema, and cotton wool spots.

stem:
A 55-year-old high myope complains of sudden onset of multiple new floaters, flashes of light (photopsia),
and a dark 'curtain-like' shadow descending across the visual field of his left eye. Fundoscopy reveals a
greyish elevated retina with a red horseshoe break. What type of retinal detachment is this?
rationale:
Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD) is caused by a full-thickness retinal break (horseshoe tear) allowing
liquefied vitreous into the subretinal space, presenting with flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect.

stem:
On examination of a patient with suspected retinal tear, tiny brownish pigment granules are observed
floating in the anterior vitreous ('tobacco dust'). What is this pathognomonic clinical sign called?
rationale:
Shafer's sign ('tobacco dust') refers to released retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells floating in the anterior vitreous,
pathognomonic for a full-thickness retinal tear.

stem:
A 20-year-old male complains of progressive night blindness (nyctalopia) and loss of peripheral vision
(tunnel vision). Fundoscopy reveals bone-spicule pigment deposits in the mid-peripheral retina, waxy disc
pallor, and arteriolar attenuation. What is the diagnosis?
rationale:
Retinitis Pigmentosa presents with the classic triad: (1) bone-spicule intraretinal pigmentation in mid-periphery, (2) waxy
pallor of the optic disc, and (3) retinal arteriolar attenuation, presenting with night blindness.

stem:
An 18-month-old child is brought by his mother after she noticed a white pupillary reflex ('cat's eye reflex' /
leukocoria) in photos of the child's right eye. What is the most dangerous, life-threatening intraocular
malignancy of childhood to rule out?
rationale:
Retinoblastoma is the most common primary malignant intraocular tumor of childhood and the single most critical
life-threatening cause of leukocoria to rule out urgently.

stem:
Histological examination of a enucleated eyespecimen with retinoblastoma shows true rosettes composed
of tumor cells arranged around a central lumen containing cytoplasmic processes of photoreceptors. What are
these characteristic rosettes called?
rationale:
Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are pathognomonic for retinoblastoma, representing specific photoreceptor differentiation
(Homer Wright rosettes are non-specific neuroblastic rosettes).

stem:
According to Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) guidelines, what is the treatment of
choice for Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with high-risk characteristics (NVD or NVE with vitreous
hemorrhage)?
rationale:
Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) is the gold standard treatment for Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy, destroying
ischemic peripheral retina to reduce VEGF production and regress neovascularization.

stem:
What is the primary cause of Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) in patients with long-standing
Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy?

options.B: Contraction of fibrovascular membranes pulling sensory retina off RPE
options.E: Subretinal fluid accumulation from choroidal melanoma

rationale:
Tractional Retinal Detachment in PDR is caused by progressive contraction of fibrovascular membranes along vascular
arcades, pulling the neurosensory retina away from underlying RPE.

stem:
A 72-year-old female complains of distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) and central vision loss.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) reveals choroidal neovascularization (CNV) with subretinal fluid in the
macula. What is the first-line treatment for wet Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)?

options.B: Oral zinc and vitamin supplementation only

rationale:
Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) are the primary standard of care to regress
Choroidal Neovascular Membranes (CNVM) in wet AMD.

stem:
What is the primary anatomical component of Cloquet's canal (Hyaloid canal) running through the central
vitreous cavity from the optic disc to the posterior lens capsule in embryonic life?

options.E: Primary vitreous containing fetal hyaloid artery remnant

rationale:
Cloquet's canal is the central transparent vestigial pathway in the vitreous body representing the original canal occupied
by the fetal hyaloid artery (primary vitreous).

stem:
Which anatomical site represents the STRONGEST physiological attachment of the vitreous body to the
underlying retina?

options.A: Ligament of Weiger at posterior lens capsule
options.E: Vitreous base across the ora serrata

rationale:
The vitreous base (straddling the ora serrata and posterior pars plana) is the firmest and strongest anatomical attachment
of the vitreous.

stem:
A systemic patient with subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) presents with retinal hemorrhages featuring
pale or white central spots composed of platelet-fibrin thrombi. What are these hemorrhages called?
rationale:
Roth's spots are retinal hemorrhages with pale white centers (leukemic cells or fibrin thrombi) classically associated with
Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis (SBE) and leukemia.

stem: What is the fundamental mechanism of visual loss in Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO)?
rationale:
Macular edema (along with macular ischemia) is the leading cause of reduced visual acuity in both branch and central
retinal vein occlusions.

stem: What is the EARLIEST clinical hallmark of active anterior uveitis observed during slit-lamp biomicroscopy?
rationale:
Breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier allows protein leakage into the anterior chamber, appearing as aqueous flare
(scattering of light beam / Tyndall effect), which is the earliest sign of anterior uveitis.

stem:
Large, greasy 'mutton-fat' Keratic Precipitates (KPs) on the corneal endothelium composed of epithelioid
cells and macrophages are pathognomonic for:
rationale:
Mutton-fat KPs are large inflammatory deposits composed of epithelioid histiocytes and macrophages, pathognomonic for
Granulomatous uveitis (e.g., Sarcoidosis, TB, Syphilis).

stem: Small inflammatory nodules located specifically at the pupillary margin of the iris in uveitis are known as:
rationale:
Koeppe nodules occur at the pupillary border, whereas Busacca nodules occur on the anterior surface/stroma of the iris
in granulomatous uveitis.

stem:
A 30-year-old patient presents with chronic unilateral low-grade iridocyclitis, heterochromia iridis (affected
eye paler), stellate KPs scattered across the entire endothelium, and early cataract formation, but completely
LACKS posterior synechiae. What is the diagnosis?
rationale:
Fuchs' Heterochromic Iridocyclitis is characteristically unilateral, asymptomatic/mild, with iris heterochromia, diffusely
distributed stellate KPs, cataract, glaucoma, and notable ABSENCE of posterior synechiae.

stem:
A immunocompromised AIDS patient presents with severe vision loss. Ophthalmoscopy reveals extensive
full-thickness yellow-white retinal necrosis accompanied by prominent hemorrhages, described as a 'pizza-pie'
or 'splashed tomato' fundus. What is the causative pathogen?
rationale:
CMV retinitis in advanced HIV/AIDS presents with necrotizing retinitis with hemorrhage, classically described as
'pizza-pie' or 'crushed tomato' appearance.

stem:
A patient with focal retinochoroiditis presents with a severe vitreous haze overlying a yellowish retinal
lesion, described as the classic 'headlight in the fog' sign on fundoscopy. What is the primary diagnosis?
rationale:
Ocular toxoplasmosis (recurrent congenital infection) produces focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis with intense local vitritis,
giving the 'headlight in the fog' appearance.

stem:
A patient sustains a penetrating injury to the ciliary body of the left eye. Four weeks later, BOTH eyes
develop severe granulomatous panuveitis. What is this life-threatening autoimmune condition called?
rationale:
Sympathetic Ophthalmitis is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis occurring after penetrating trauma to one eye (exciting
eye) exposing uveoretinal autoantigens, which triggers autoimmune attack in the uninjured eye (sympathizing eye).

stem:
Multiple retinal perivascular exudates resembling 'candle-wax drippings' (taches de bougie) on fundus
examination are characteristic of ocular involvement in:
rationale:
Sarcoidosis produces retinal periphlebitis with waxy, candle-wax dripping exudates ('taches de bougie') along retinal
veins.

stem:
A 2-day-old neonate presents with severe hyperacute bilateral purulent conjunctivitis, marked eyelid
edema, and chemosis. Gram stain of the discharge shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. What is the
causative organism?
rationale:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes hyperacute ophthalmia neonatorum within 2-5 days of birth, featuring profuse purulent
discharge and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci.

stem:
What is the single most common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis (Ophthalmia Neonatorum) presenting
between 5 to 14 days after birth?
rationale:
Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars D-K) is the commonest infectious cause of ophthalmia neonatorum, typically
manifesting 5 to 14 days post-delivery.

stem:
A 10-year-old boy presents with intense bilateral itching, ropy mucous discharge, and photophobia during
summer months. Slit-lamp exam reveals giant 'cobblestone' papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva and
Horner-Trantas spots at the limbus. What is the diagnosis?
rationale:
Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC / Spring catarrh) affects young males seasonally, featuring cobblestone papillae on
upper tarsal conjunctiva and Horner-Trantas spots (eosinophil dots at limbus).

stem:
In Trachoma (caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars A, B, Ba, C), healed shallow limbal depressions
remaining after regression of limbal follicles are known as:
rationale:
Herbert's pits are pathognomonic cicatricial oval depressions at the limbus resulting from healed lymphoid follicles in
chronic trachoma.

stem: What is 'Arlt's line' in the context of chronic Trachoma staging?

options.A: A line of pigment on corneal endothelium
options.B: A row of iron deposits in the cornea
options.D: A vascular pannus extending across upper cornea
options.E: A horizontal band of conjunctival scarring at the sulcus subtarsalis of the upper eyelid

rationale:
Arlt's line is a linear band of conjunctival scar tissue located at the sulcus subtarsalis parallel to the upper eyelid margin in
trachoma stage 3.

stem:
Triangular, foamy, silvery-white keratinized patches located on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus in a
malnourished child are called:
rationale:
Bitot's spots are foamy keratinized conjunctival deposits caused by Corynebacterium xerosis buildup, pathognomonic for
Vitamin A deficiency (Xerophthalmia stage X1B).

stem:
A wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva extending onto the medial limbus and cornea,
destroying Bowman's membrane, is termed a:
rationale:
Pterygium is a triangular wing-shaped fibrovascular conjunctival encroachment onto the cornea caused by UV light
exposure and elastotic degeneration.

stem: What is the fundamental clinical difference between a true Pterygium and a Pseudopterygium?

options.A: True pterygium is caused by trauma; pseudopterygium by UV light
options.B: A probe CAN be passed under the neck of a pseudopterygium, but CANNOT be passed under a true pterygium
options.D: Pseudopterygium progresses rapidly across cornea; true pterygium never moves
options.E: Pterygium only occurs on temporal side; pseudopterygium on nasal side

rationale:
A probe test distinguishes them: a probe CAN easily pass under the neck of a pseudopterygium (adhesion of conjunctiva
following burn/ulcer), whereas it CANNOT pass under a true pterygium due to adherence throughout.

stem:
A 48-year-old male presents with gradual peripheral vision loss. Visual field perimetry demonstrates a
classic bitemporal hemianopia. Where is the lesion located?
rationale:
A lesion compressing the optic chiasm (such as a pituitary adenoma) interrupts decussating nasal retinal nerve fibers,
producing a bitemporal hemianopia.

stem:
A patient involved in a motor vehicle accident suffers a complete transection of the Right Optic Tract. What
visual field defect is produced?
rationale:
A right optic tract lesion carrying temporal fibers from right eye and nasal fibers from left eye causes a contralateral (Left)
Homonymous Hemianopia.

stem:
A lesion located specifically in 'Meyer's loop' of the temporal optic radiation produces which visual field
defect?

options.A: Homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
options.E: Homonymous inferior quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')

rationale:
Meyer's loop fibers travel forward in the temporal lobe; lesions here cause a contralateral Homonymous Superior
Quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

stem:
During the Swinging Flashlight Test, shining light into the right eye causes moderate pupillary constriction,
but swinging light directly to the left eye causes BOTH pupils to paradoxically dilate. What is this sign?

options.D: Marcus Gunn pupil (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect - RAPD)

rationale:
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) indicates incomplete optic nerve or severe retinal lesion in
the affected eye, resulting in paradoxical dilation during swinging flashlight test.

stem:
Bilateral small, irregular pupils that demonstrate Light-Near Dissociation (pupils constrict during
accommodation/near reflex, but do NOT react to light) are pathognomonic for neurosyphilis. What are these
pupils called?
rationale:
Argyll Robertson pupils are small, bilateral, irregular pupils that accommodate but do NOT react to light ('ARP =
Accommodation Reflex Present, Light Reflex Absent'), pathognomonic for neurosyphilis.

stem:
A 30-year-old female presents with a unilateral dilated pupil that reacts very slowly (tonically) to near stimuli
and demonstrates cholinergic supersensitivity (constricting to 0.125% dilute pilocarpine). What is the
diagnosis?
rationale:
Adie's tonic pupil (ciliary ganglion denervation) features a light-near dissociated dilated pupil showing denervation
supersensitivity to weak (0.125%) pilocarpine.

stem:
What is the classic clinical triad of Horner's Syndrome (caused by disruption of sympathetic nerve supply
to the eye)?

options.E: Partial ptosis, miosis, ipsilateral facial anhidrosis

rationale:
Horner's syndrome triad consists of: (1) partial ptosis (Muller's muscle paralysis), (2) miosis (pupillodilator paralysis), and
(3) ipsilateral facial anhidrosis (sweat gland loss).

stem:
A 6-year-old child presents with severe congenital ptosis of the upper eyelid covering the pupil. On
examination, Levator Palpebrae Superioris (LPS) action is measured at 2 mm (poor levator function). Bell's
phenomenon is normal. What is the surgical procedure of choice?
rationale:
In severe ptosis with poor LPS function (<4 mm), levator resection is ineffective; a Frontalis Sling operation connecting
tarsal plate to frontalis muscle is indicated.

stem:
A 35-year-old patient presents with a painless, hard, non-tender nodule in the upper eyelid of 3 months
duration. Biopsy shows chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland. What is this lesion
called?
rationale: A Chalazion is a chronic sterile lipogranulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland resulting from duct obstruction.

stem:
An acute focal purulent infection of a Zeis or Moll gland located at the lash margin of the eyelid, presenting
as a painful, red swelling, is called a:
rationale:
An External Hordeolum (Stye) is an acute suppurative inflammation of an eyelash follicle and its associated Zeis
(sebaceous) or Moll (sweat) gland.

stem:
A 10-month-old infant is brought with persistent epiphora and sticky discharge from the right eye since
birth. Crigler digital massage has failed. What is the most common anatomical site of obstruction in Congenital
Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO)?

options.B: Valve of Hasner at lower end of nasolacrimal duct

rationale:
CNLDO is most commonly caused by delayed recanalization or persistent mucosal membrane at the Valve of Hasner at
the inferior meatal opening of the NLD.

stem:
What is the next management step for Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction in a 12-month-old infant
when lacrimal massage has proven unsuccessful?

options.B: Intubation with silicon tube at 20 years
options.E: Nasolacrimal duct probing under general anesthesia

rationale:
If CNLDO fails to resolve with digital massage by 10-12 months of age, nasolacrimal duct probing under general
anesthesia is the treatment of choice (90%+ success).

stem:
A 45-year-old female presents with acute pain, redness, and swelling over the medial canthus area below
the medial palpebral ligament. Pressing over the lacrimal sac produces purulent discharge from the puncta.
What is the diagnosis?
rationale:
Acute Dacryocystitis is acute inflammation/infection of the lacrimal sac, presenting with pain, erythema, and swelling at
the inner canthus below medial palpebral ligament.

stem:
What is the surgical procedure of choice for Chronic Dacryocystitis with nasolacrimal duct obstruction in
an adult, which restores tear drainage into the middle nasal meatus?
rationale:
Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) creates a surgical anastomosis between the lacrimal sac and nasal mucosa of the middle
nasal meatus to bypass an obstructed NLD.

stem:
A female patient presents with axial proptosis, lid retraction in primary gaze (Dalrymple's sign), and lid lag
on downgaze (Von Graefe's sign). What is the underlying condition?
rationale:
Thyroid Eye Disease (Graves' orbitopathy) is the commonest cause of adult bilateral/unilateral proptosis, featuring
Dalrymple's sign (lid retraction) and Von Graefe's sign (lid lag).

stem:
What is the most common cause of proptosis in children accompanied by fever, severe pain, restricted
painful ocular movements, and RAPD?
rationale:
Orbital cellulitis (often secondary to ethmoid sinusitis) is an ophthalmic emergency presenting in children with painful
proptosis, fever, ophthalmoplegia, and decreased vision.

stem: What anatomical landmark separates Preseptal Cellulitis from true Orbital Cellulitis?
rationale:
The Orbital Septum is a key fibrous barrier extending from orbital margins to tarsal plates; infections anterior to it are
preseptal, whereas those posterior are orbital cellulitis.

stem:
A 20-year-old student experiences blurred distant vision, but clear near vision. Parallel rays of light entering
the unaccommodated eye focus in FRONT of the retina. What is this refractive error?
rationale:
Myopia (nearsightedness) occurs when parallel light rays focus in front of the retina, corrected using concave (minus)
spherical lenses.

stem:
What type of optical lens is used to correct Hypermetropia (farsightedness), where parallel rays focus
behind the retina?
rationale:
Hypermetropia is corrected with converging Convex (plus) spherical lenses that shift the focal point forward onto the
retina.

stem:
A 48-year-old patient reports difficulty reading small print at normal reading distance. This age-related
physiological loss of accommodation due to decreased lens elasticity is termed:
rationale:
Presbyopia is the progressive age-related decline in accommodative amplitude due to sclerosis of crystalline lens and
ciliary muscle weakening, corrected with convex plus add lenses.

stem:
What type of lens is required to correct Astigmatism, a condition where light rays passing through different
meridians fail to focus at a single focal point?
rationale: Astigmatism (unequal corneal curvature in different meridians) is corrected using Cylindrical or Toric lenses.

stem:
A worker accidentally splashes sodium hydroxide (alkali/quicklime) into his right eye. What is the
immediate, mandatory FIRST AID intervention required at the workplace/emergency room?

options.A: Perform immediate, copious eye irrigation with water or saline for 15-30 minutes

rationale:
Alkali burns cause rapid liquefactive necrosis penetrating deep tissues. Immediate, prolonged irrigation for 15-30 minutes
takes priority over all diagnostic procedures.

stem:
Following a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor (maxillary bone) from a fist injury, which extraocular
muscle is most commonly trapped in the fracture site, restricting upward gaze?
rationale:
Orbital floor blowout fractures commonly trap the Inferior Rectus muscle (and inferior oblique), causing diplopia on
vertical gaze and restricted elevation.

stem:
A patient presents with vertical diplopia that worsens on downgaze and tilt to the affected side. On
examination, the eye is hypertropic. Which cranial nerve is paralyzed?
rationale:
Trochlear (CN IV) nerve palsy causes weakness of the Superior Oblique muscle, presenting with vertical diplopia that
worsens on downgaze and tilting head toward affected side.

stem:
A child is diagnosed with non-paralytic convergent squint (Esotropia). What is the primary cause of
'Accommodative Esotropia' in young children?
rationale:
Uncorrected high hypermetropia requires excessive accommodation to clear images, triggering excessive AC/A ratio
accommodation-convergence and inward deviation (Esotropia).

stem:
Using the high-yield embryology mnemonic LEVL, which ocular structure is derived from SURFACE
ECTODERM during embryonic development?

options.B: Epithelium of cornea and Crystalline Lens

rationale:
Surface ectoderm gives rise to the crystalline lens, corneal/conjunctival epithelium, lacrimal gland, and eyelid epidermis
(Mnemonic LEVL: Lens, Epithelium, Vitreous, Lacrimal).

stem: The sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles of the iris originate from which embryonic germ layer?
rationale:
Uniquely, the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles are derived from Neural Ectoderm of the optic cup (unlike most
intraocular muscles which derive from neural crest/mesoderm).
